title: City of clayton sales tax measure
question: To provide local funding to maintain City of Clayton programs, services, and facilities, including: police services, traffic enforcement and road safety, road and sidewalk improvements, enhance library and recreation opportunities, park maintenance, recruitment and retention of city employees and other city services, shall the City of Clayton levy a 1% sales tax until ended by voters generating approximately $1,000,000 annually, subject to public review, the annual audit and all funds benefitting Clayton?
analysis: On June 16, 2026, the City Council voted unanimously to place Measure M on the November 3, 2026 General Municipal Election ballot.

If approved by a majority of Clayton voters, this Measure would authorize a one percent (1%) retail transactions and use (sales) tax within the City of Clayton. A one percent (1%) rate equates to an extra $1 per $100 purchased. It is estimated that Measure M will provide an additional $1,000,000 in annual local funding that could be used for City of Clayton programs, services and facilities, including police services, traffic enforcement and road safety programs, road and sidewalk improvements, enhancing library and recreation services, park maintenance, and recruitment and retention of City employees. This tax would be a “general tax,” meaning that revenues raised from the tax would go into the City’s general fund to pay for any lawful City program, improvement, or service.

The California Constitution (Proposition 218) and Revenue and Taxation Code section 7285.9 authorize the City to levy a general transactions and use/sales tax at a rate of one percent (1%) so long as the tax is approved by a majority of the voters voting in an election on that issue. If approved, the tax would become operative on April 1, 2027 and remain in effect until repealed by voters at a subsequent election.

The tax would be paid in addition to current sales taxes and would be collected at the same time and in the same manner as existing sales taxes. All revenues raised by the tax would remain in the City and would not be shared with the State, County or any other agency.
A “yes” vote on Measure M will authorize the 1% transactions and use (sales) tax.
A “no” vote on Measure M will not authorize the 1% transactions and use (sales) tax.
arg_for: Measure M is an investment in Clayton’s quality of life designed to protect our city’s future.
Clayton will soon be facing a long-term structural deficit of $1.18 million due to rising costs of delivering essential services.

This deficit means that without action, the City will struggle to sustain our current police services, repair our streets and sidewalks, preserve parks and recreation programs, and maintain aging infrastructure.

Measure M offers a long-term solution to our deficit through a 1% sales tax increase. Projections estimate this will generate $1 million annually. This tax increase will ensure the City has the resources to continue delivering the quality services residents depend on.
Since Clayton’s founding, City leaders have always fought to avoid tax increases.

Before proposing Measure M, the City exhausted every other available means of generating new revenue. This included updating fees, reorganizing staff, and reducing service contracts. Those measures have helped, but are simply not enough to close our deficit.
The City does not propose this lightly. Measure M would be our first sales tax increase in the City’s sixty-two year history, which is why Clayton’s sales tax rate is among the lowest in the County.

Measure M is a local decision designed to meet local priorities. Should residents choose to approve Measure M, all of the resulting funds would remain accountable to residents and under the control of the City, not the County or State. That means 100% of all revenues generated stay in Clayton.
Clayton is a special community defined by safe neighborhoods, well-maintained parks, and a high quality of life.
By acting now, we can protect the services that make Clayton a desirable place to live, work, and raise a family while avoiding more difficult and expensive choices later.
Kim Trupiano, Councilmember
Holly Tillman, Councilmember
Jeff Wan, Mayor
Richard G. Enea, Vice-Mayor
Jim Diaz, Councilmember
arg_against: Vote No on the 1% Clayton Sales Tax. We sent a message in June. Now, let’s stand firm in November.
• In June 2026, Clayton residents joined voters across Contra Costa County to decisively defeat Measure B, a 0.625% sales tax hike. In Clayton, 69% of voters wisely said No to Measure B.

• The message from our community was clear: inflation and the cost of living are hurting families, and we cannot afford more taxes. Yet, just weeks later, the Clayton City Council voted 5-0 to push an even larger 1% tax increase onto the November ballot.
• This proposal ignores the clear financial mandate Clayton citizens just delivered at the polls.

• Clayton’s overall sales tax rate is an already high 8.75%; Measure M would spike that rate to 9.75% , punishing working families and fixed-income seniors. If Measure RTM also passes, our total rate would reach 10.25%.
Fuel Staff Pay Hikes:
• Our politicians have no set agreement for how the proposed tax hike will be used.

• Ultimately, this revenue increase to the general fund will likely be absorbed by rising city salaries, continuing to leave deferred infrastructure neglected and triggering future tax hikes to pay for actual community needs.
A Losing Compensation Race:

• Government salaries and employee benefits have risen significantly since the pandemic, while the private sector faces layoffs. Between 2019 and 2025, total Clayton employee compensation rose 37%, well ahead of Bay Area consumer price inflation.
• Setting Clayton’s small-town employee salaries to other city governments ensures that future spending will likely exceed revenues, requiring more tax increases.
No End in Sight:
• Unlike the failed Measure B, which was set to expire after 5 years, Clayton’s Measure M is a permanent tax hike.
• Clayton government must learn to live within its means, just like Clayton families do every single day.
Keep Clayton Sensible. Vote No on Measure M.
Contra Costa Taxpayers Association, Marc D. Joffe, President
James Killoran, Credit Union Supervisory Committee Chair, Clayton
Allison Snow, Retired Healthcare Executive, Clayton
Nancy Topp, CPA/CFO, Clayton
Bill Calkins, Clayton Resident

title: Citywide landscape maintenance extension and alteration of rate of existing special tax
question: Shall the measure to fund on-going trail system operations and maintenance, roadway landscaping, open space weed abatement, and related services of the Clayton Community Facility District No. 2007-1 (Citywide Landscape Maintenance) by extending the special tax for ten years and amending its rate and methodology to $354.45/year per residential parcel and $354.45/year per non-residential acre, including annual inflationary adjustments, subject to citizen’s committee oversight, be approved?
analysis: The City of Clayton has established Community Facilities District 2007-1 within the City (“CFD”), which is authorized to levy a special parcel tax on real property within the CFD to fund City trail system operations and maintenance, roadway landscaping, open space weed abatement, and related services. Pursuant to City Measure “H”, the CFD currently levies the tax at the annual rate of $312.84 per residential parcel and $312.84 per acre, or fraction thereof, for non-residential parcels. The tax started collection on July 1, 2007 and will expire on June 30, 2027, unless extended by voters.

After conducting a noticed public hearing on July 7, 2026, the City Council unanimously voted to place Measure N on the November 3, 2026 General Municipal Election ballot. It proposes to extend the CFD parcel tax for ten (10) years, with a new expiration date of June 30, 2037. It also proposes to increase the annual parcel tax rate, starting July 1, 2027, to $354.45 per residential parcel and $354.45 per acre, or fraction thereof, for non-residential parcels.

The Measure allows the City Council to increase the tax rate, starting July 1, 2028 and in each fiscal year thereafter by the applicable Consumer Price Index, with a 3% annual cap, after making such a determination at a regular public meeting and after receiving a prior recommendation from the City’s Citizens’ Trails and Landscaping Committee.

The tax will expire on June 30, 2037, unless further extended by Clayton voters at a future election. Measure N does not change the purposes of the parcel tax. Tax revenues will continue to be deposited into a special City fund and used solely to fund City trail system operations and maintenance, roadway landscaping, open space weed abatement, and related services.

Measure N incorporates citizen’s committee oversight. This CFD parcel tax would be collected in the same time and manner and subject to the same requirements as other property taxes fixed and collected by the County of Contra Costa on behalf of the City of Clayton.
Measure N requires the approval of two-thirds (2/3) of Clayton voters voting on the Measure to pass.
A “yes” vote on Measure N will approve this CFD parcel tax.
A “no” vote on Measure N will not approve this CFD parcel tax.
arg_for: In 1997, Clayton established the Trails and Landscape Maintenance District (District) to fund the maintenance of trails, open space, weed abatement, firebreaks, and roadside landscaping. A 10-year parcel tax was adopted, providing dedicated funding for Clayton’s landscaping.

In 2007, a citizens’ Blue Ribbon Committee reviewed the District’s successes and challenges. The importance of Clayton’s “Front Yard” was reaffirmed, and a new plan was recommended. It included a Trails and Landscape Committee (TLC), a citizen advisory body appointed by the City Council, to advise the Council and staff on maintenance, improvements, and financial matters related to the Landscape Maintenance District (LMD). Voters overwhelmingly extended the parcel tax in 2007 and 2017, ensuring continued investment in Clayton’s medians, parks, trails, and open spaces.

In FY 2026-2027, residents currently pay $312.84/year per parcel and nonresidents $312.84/per acre or fraction thereof. The LMD maintains approximately 2 million square feet of roadway landscaping, 40,700 square feet of lawns and flowerbeds, 515 acres of open space, 27 miles of trails, 50 street islands and medians, and roughly 3,000 City trees. The LMD funds also support critical fire mitigation efforts in open spaces and around trails, including weed abatement. Evolving fire safety requirements are expected to increase these costs, making dedicated funding increasingly important.

Measure N includes a one-time, 10% reserve fee dedicated to capital improvements and longstanding deferred maintenance. For FY 2027-2028, residents will pay no more than $354.45/year per parcel and nonresidents $354.45/year per acre or fraction thereof, generating $1.5 million annually through 2037, with continued oversight by the TLC.
Clayton’s modest General Fund cannot adequately fund public landscaping and trails. Without this dedicated funding, maintenance would rapidly decline, forever changing Clayton’s beauty and character.
Please support Measure N and essential fire mitigation efforts, and preserve Clayton’s landscaping, trails, open spaces, and community character for future generations.
Holly Tillman, Councilmember
Kim Trupiano, Councilmember
Richard G. Enea, Vice-Mayor
Jeff Wan, Mayor
Jim Diaz, Councilmember
arg_against: We know from experience or hearsay (depending on age) that last midcentury, two dimes would buy a gallon of gas or two scoops of ice cream; ten dimes could buy 6 basic hamburgers. If the dimes are silver, they still do. But the digital and paper currencies aren’t doing as well.
You may be aware that Japan was bailed out by the U.S. because they are our biggest buyer of Treasurys and need money, but if they sell our debt, it devalues faster.
What does this have to do with this proposed Special Tax? It would rise with inflation. The United States of America is inflating like crazy, and they’re just getting started.
The next ten years are likely to be challenging for everyone.
Perhaps the landscaping budget could be funded by sponsorships, voluntary neighborhood workdays, fundraisers.
Also bad: spending public funds to defend against violations of election code.
California Elections Code section 13119(a) requires ballots to use this language:
“Shall the measure (stating the nature thereof) be adopted?”
“The nature thereof” does not mean “why,” or “how,” or “for whom,” or anything other than “what is the nature” of the measure being adopted.

Contra Costa County wrote a ballot question recently. It was ruled “prejudicial and argumentative” in Superior Court. The court ordered offending language removed, including “independent citizens oversight.”
Section 9051(e) requires it “shall neither be an argument, nor be likely to create prejudice, for or against the proposed measure.”
Clayton’s Measure N ballot question lists benefits, not costs like pay-raises; it is not neutral.

If you don’t like public funds spent defending violations, the best way to save court costs and stop cheating, is vote “No” every time you see a ballot question containing sales pitches. Save that for the argument.
Libertarian Party of Contra Costa County, Sandra Kallander, Chair

title: Business license tax update
question: To protect City of Concord services/ensure smaller businesses pay less than larger businesses, shall the measure be adopted to: repair potholes on neighborhood and major streets; maintain 9-1-1 emergency response; keep parks/playgrounds safe/clean; relieve traffic congestion along major corridors; maintain senior/youth programs; for general government use; by updating Concord’s 37-year-old business license rates to 0.1% of gross receipts until ended by voters, providing an additional $2,900,000 annually, requiring independent citizen oversight?
analysis: The Concord City Council has placed Measure O (“Business License Tax Simplification Ballot Measure”) on the ballot. Concord’s existing gross receipts business license tax rate schedule, based on graduated tiers of gross receipts, with rates that become progressively lower from 0.1% to 0.03% as business gross receipts increase, has remained substantially unchanged for approximately 40 years. Measure O would replace those tiered rates with a single uniform rate of one tenth of one percent (0.1%) of gross receipts for gross receipts-based businesses. Measure O would expand the small business exemption for students and seniors making less than $3,600 to any business making less than $5,000. Neither the existing gross receipts tax rates nor the rates as amended by Measure O contain inflation adjustments. Measure O also clarifies the initial due and delinquency dates for tax payments; clarifies that refund claims must be submitted within one year of payment consistent with state law; subjects the existing $25 minimum tax to inflationary adjustments; and imposes interest of 1.5% per month on delinquent amounts.

Because Measure O does not legally restrict use of the tax revenues to any specific purpose, it is a “general tax.” The tax proceeds would be deposited in Concord’s general fund and may be used for any valid governmental purpose, including: pothole repair and street maintenance, 911 emergency response, park and playground upkeep, traffic congestion relief, and senior and youth programs. It is an independent source of revenue for Concord that neither Sacramento nor the federal government can take.

Measure O requires the City’s independent auditors to prepare a publicly available annual report on the collection, management, and expenditure of $2.9 million of the additional revenue generated by Measure O. Concord’s existing Measure V Citizens’ Oversight Committee would review/report on the receipt/expenditure of those funds.

Business license tax is paid only by businesses operating in Concord and not by residents who are not business owners. Under current law, smaller businesses subject to the general gross receipts tax with lower gross receipts pay a higher effective tax rate than larger businesses with higher gross receipts because the tax rate decreases at each successive tier.

Measure O would eliminate that tiered structure and apply the same 0.1% rate to all general gross receipts taxed businesses, regardless of size. Measure O would not change the rates for manufacturing, specified professions and trades, apartments, hotels, motels, contractors, or other specifically identified business categories.

Measure O will be approved if it receives a simple majority of “Yes” votes. Measure O would terminate when repealed by Concord voters. If Measure O is not approved, the existing tiered gross receipts business license tax rates and exemption for only student/senior businesses making under $3,600 (rather than any business making $5,000 or less) in annual gross receipts would remain in place; due-date, delinquency date, and refund claim date clarifications would not be made; the $25 minimum tax would not be subject to inflationary adjustments; and interest on delinquent amounts would not be imposed.
A “Yes” vote is a vote in favor of Measure O.
A “No” vote is a vote against Measure O.
Dated: August 13, 2026
Susanne Meyer Brown
City Attorney
City of Concord
arg_for: Vote Yes on O – Maintain Concord’s safety and quality of life!

Yes on O simplifies and updates Concord’s nearly 40-year-old business license structure to ensure that large businesses are paying their fair share, and smaller businesses are not unfairly shouldering the cost of keeping Concord a safe, well-maintained community. Measure O is not a tax on homeowners or residents. Measure O simply updates an outdated business tax structure.
Yes on O will:
• Repair potholes, neighborhood and major city streets
• Maintain 9-1-1 emergency response
• Keep parks/playgrounds safe and clean for kids
• Relieve traffic congestion along major corridors
• Maintain senior and youth programs

Yes on O requires strict transparency and accountability – including Independent Citizens Oversight, public disclosure of all spending, financial audits, and yearly reports to the community to ensure that all funds are spent locally and as promised.
Yes on O ensures local control over local dollars for our own local needs. Not a penny can be taken by the state.

We need Yes on O . Did you know? Concord has approximately 65 million square feet of public streets to maintain and keep safe! In an accident, disaster or medical emergency, Measure O helps ensure rapid 9-1-1 emergency services are ready when we need them the most, including first responders who must safely and quickly reach people that need help.

Vote Yes on O ! By simplifying the business license structure, Measure O ensures smaller businesses, homeowners, and residents aren’t unfairly shouldering the cost of vital local services like public safety, roads, parks, and emergency response.
Let’s keep Concord safe and maintain our quality of life – Join a unanimous City Council, local businesses, community leaders, and neighbors in voting Yes on O!
Zulay Loftin, Owner, Loftin Dental
Mary Totah, Owner, Parma Deli
Antonio Barragan, Store Manager, Las Montanas Supermarket
Wes Andreen, Owner, Just Trains
Mohamed Habib Jacifi, Owner, Luna Restaurant
arg_against: Who Pays?
• The City claims residents who aren’t business owners won’t pay more. Businesses rarely absorb new costs passively — they pass them along through higher prices at the shops,
restaurants, and services you use every day.
• A tax on business is, in actual effect, a tax on everyone who spends money in Concord.
Where does the money go?
• This measure funds the General Fund, not a locked account earmarked specifically for roads or emergency response.
• Like past measures, future City Councils retain full discretion over how the money is actually spent, regardless of what’s advertised now.
Right time?
• Concord voters are already facing a regional transit sales tax and other county measures on this same ballot. Stacking another new tax on top — even one branded as
“modernization” — adds to a real cumulative burden on households and businesses at a moment when affordability is already strained.
Startup Penalties?
• New companies losing money still owe the tax because the levy ignores production costs
Well Written?
• This overhaul of a 40-year-old structure is significant and deserves more scrutiny than a single election cycle allows.
• The rewrite must include a truly independent, binding oversight and sunset mechanism without which voters are being asked to trust the outcome rather than control it.
Vote No, and ask the City to return with a plan that includes real accountability — a hard spending lock, a sunset date, and full transparency — before asking Concord to pay more.
No on O!
Contra Costa Taxpayers Assn, Cynthia Johnson, Co-Treasurer
Jennifer Wang-Filomeo, Concord Resident
Eric Rotsten, Real Estate Broker

title: Sales tax
question: Shall the measure providing Hercules with locally controlled funding to maintain financial stability/general city services, such as fast 911 response; neighborhood police patrols; water quality standards; keeping public areas/parks safe/ clean; repairing deteriorating streets/potholes; and retaining/attracting local businesses, by establishing a one-cent (1%) sales tax generating approximately $4,000,000 annually until ended by voters; requiring audits, public disclosure, and funds only for Hercules, be adopted?
analysis: This measure (the “Hercules Public Safety/ Financial Stability Measure”) would add Chapter 11 to Title 8 to the Hercules Municipal Code and would impose a transactions and use tax, commonly known as a sales tax, of up to 1% in the City of Hercules.

The tax would be imposed on the sale or use of tangible personal property in the City. The tax would be administered by the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration, which administers all sales and use taxes and transactions and use taxes in California.

The tax would be collected in addition to the existing sales and use and transactions and use taxes already imposed by the State of California, Contra Costa County, and BART in the City of Hercules. It would also be collected in addition to the City’s existing transactions and use tax in Chapter 9 of Title 8 of the Hercules Municipal Code. The current combined rate for all sales and use and transactions and use taxes in Hercules is 9.25%.
Groceries and prescription medicines would be exempt from the tax.
The proposed tax is estimated to generate $4,000,000 per year, and the California Constitution prohibits the State from taking this revenue from the City.

The proposed tax is a general tax, which means the revenues could be used by the City for any lawful municipal purpose, such as 911 response, neighborhood police patrols, water quality standards, keeping public areas and parks safe and clean, repairing deteriorating streets and fixing potholes, and retaining and attracting local businesses.
If approved, the tax would begin to be collected on April 1, 2027 and would continue to be collected until repealed.
The tax would be imposed at a rate of 1%, unless state law limits the tax rate to a lower rate, in which case it would be imposed at the maximum rate allowed under the law, but no more than 1%

Revenues collected under this tax will be subject to an independent financial audit conducted annually by a certified public accountant, and the expenditure of the revenues will be stated in the annual budget. Both the annual audit and the budget will be presented and reviewed by the Hercules City Council in an open public meeting.
The measure was placed on the ballot by the Hercules City Council. The measure will take effect if a majority (50% plus 1) of voters voting on the measure vote “Yes.”
s/Christine Crowl, City Attorney, City of Hercules
arg_for: If you care about Public Safety and Health in Hercules, vote Yes on P!

Hercules is finally a place where people want to live and raise their families. Voting Yes on P maintains our community momentum and the essential City services that make Hercules a safe, well-maintained place to live during a time of economic and national uncertainty.
Yes on P maintains a healthy, safe and vibrant Hercules community.
Yes on P maintains fast 911 response and the police officers patrolling our neighborhoods.
Yes on P helps our City meet current water quality standards.
Yes on P keeps public areas and parks safe and clean.
Yes on P retains and attracts local businesses.

With the State facing its own major budget deficit and declining federal funding, Measure P is a critical strategy to continue to maintain Hercules’s long-term financial stability. Measure P is fiscally accountable with mandatory financial audits, yearly reports, and public disclosure to ensure its funds are spent on the community’s priorities, responsibly.
All Measure P funding must stay here in Hercules for our own local needs. Not a dime can be taken by Sacramento politicians, the County, or federal government.
Here’s what Yes on P Won’t do:
Measure P is Not a tax on your property or home.
Measure P is Not applied to food purchased as groceries or prescription medication.
Join the majority of the Hercules City Council and community leaders: Vote Yes on P: Protect our Public Safety and our Safe, Healthy Hercules!
To read the official Measure P documents, visit herculesca.gov
Hercules Police Officer’s Association, Chris Costa, President
Darrel “Jay” Tucker, President, Hercules Historical Society, Former Hercules Mayor and Council Member
Richard Mitchell, Former Hercules Planning Commissioner
Jo Ellen Marcotte, Member, Hercules Library Foundation
arg_against: Vote No on the Measure P tax hike!
Everything in and around Hercules costs more, and now the City Council wants to add another 1% to the price of gas, school supplies, clothes, and other essentials.
A higher tax on nearly everything you buy:
• Measure P raises Hercules’ sales tax from 9.25% to 10.25%. Your ballot also carries a separate 0.5% regional transit tax. If both pass, Hercules shoppers will pay 10.75%, tying El
Cerrito and Pinole for the highest sales tax in Contra Costa County, and well above the national and California averages.
• It even raises the price of a new car. California charges vehicle tax at the buyer’s home address, so Hercules residents would pay 10.75% no matter where they buy, e.g., $5,375 on a
$50,000 vehicle. You can’t escape it by shopping out of town.
• Sales taxes hit low- and middle-income families hardest. If Hercules truly values equity, why penalize those who can least afford it? If Measure P passes, shoppers can save 1.5%
on necessities simply by buying in unincorporated Rodeo or El Sobrante.
The real problem is spending, not revenue:
• Hercules’ own audited statements show General Fund spending more than doubled in a decade, from $10.2 million in 2015 to $20.7 million in 2025. Where is the money going?
• Nine city employees each received more than $200,000 in wages in 2025 according to State Controller data.
• Staff admit the retail tax base is “not robust enough to fund anything more than basic service levels.” If spending can double while services stay “basic,” the problem isn’t too little
tax money; it’s how the money is managed.
Before charging residents the highest sales tax in the county, the Council should show real spending restraint.
The sales tax in Hercules is high enough already.
Vote No on Measure P.
Contra Costa Taxpayers Association, Marc D. Joffe, President
Michael Hernandez, Hercules Resident
Michael Letcher, Hercules Resident

title: Bond measure
question: To support rapid, 911 emergency medical response, modernize and rehabilitate unsafe/deteriorating firefighter housing and facilities, including mold/asbestos abatement/removal, replace electrical systems, leaky pipes/roofs, and improve structure resiliency during disasters, shall the City of Richmond’s measure authorizing $120,000,000 in bonds at legal rates, levying an estimated average tax rate of $22.15/$100,000 of assessed valuation, averaging $7,568,158 annually while bonds are outstanding, requiring citizen oversight, audits, and spending only on approved projects, be adopted?
analysis: This measure was placed on the ballot by the Richmond City Council. It requires a two-thirds vote of the electorate to pass.

If approved, this measure would authorize the City of Richmond to issue general obligation bonds in a principal amount not to exceed $120,000,000, to be repaid through an ad valorem property tax levied on all taxable property within the City.
The proceeds of the bonds would fund:
• Repair, replacement, or reconstruction of fire stations, including seismic improvements;
• Renovation, upgrade, reconstruction, or acquisition of firefighter living quarters, including remediation of hazardous materials and improvements related to applicable building standards;
• Repair or replacement of electrical systems, roofs, plumbing, and piping at fire stations;
• Structural, seismic, and other resiliency improvements at fire stations;
• Repair, replacement, or installation of fixtures and building systems such as emergency generators, HVAC systems, and communications infrastructure; and
• Construction, renovation, upgrade, reconstruction, or acquisition of training facilities, administrative offices, apparatus bays, and other facilities supporting Fire Department operations.
The City Council retains discretion over the scope and sequencing of individual projects, and completion of all listed improvements is not guaranteed.
Bond proceeds may be used only for the acquisition or improvement of real property and fixtures, and related incidental costs, and may not be used for other municipal purposes.

The measure includes the following accountability requirements: proceeds may be spent only for the specific purposes described in the measure; proceeds will be deposited into a separate account; the City Council will appoint a Community Oversight Committee of City residents to monitor expenditure of the proceeds; the Director of Finance will file an annual report to the City Council on funds collected and expended and the status of authorized projects; and all expenditures will be subject to an annual independent financial audit.

The average tax rate to repay the bonds is projected to be $22.15 per $100,000 of assessed valuation, averaging approximately $7,568,158 annually while the bonds remain outstanding. The highest tax rate is projected to be $24.06 per $100,000 of assessed valuation, first applying in fiscal year 2028. The total debt service, including principal and interest, if all bonds are issued and sold, is estimated to be $249,749,206, with the final fiscal year in which the tax is anticipated to be collected being 2060. The Tax Rate Statement, prepared under Elections Code Section 9401, contains additional detail and is available from the Richmond City Clerk.
The maximum interest rate on the bonds would be 12 percent per annum. Bonds may be issued in one or more series as determined by the City Council.
A “YES” vote authorizes the City to issue the bonds as summarized above.
A “NO” vote does not authorize the City to issue the bonds.

This analysis summarizes the measure’s legal effect and is not an argument for or against the measure. The full text of the measure is available in the Voter Information Guide and from the Richmond City Clerk.
SHANNON MOORE
Interim City Attorney, City of Richmond
arg_for: Richmond’s emergency response infrastructure is failing us—and our first responders.

When a heart attack, stroke, serious injury, or other emergency strikes, every second counts . But our aging, undersized stations can’t accommodate enough firefighters or the latest equipment needed to respond quickly. Slower response times put residents at risk when speed is a matter of life or death.

Today, some Richmond firefighters work in seismically unsafe buildings, with cracking foundations, leaky roofs, mold, and outdated electrical systems, jeopardizing their health and safety while they work to protect ours.

Measure Q is a responsible, accountable plan to fix Richmond’s emergency response infrastructure. It authorizes $120 million in bonds to modernize and rehabilitate unsafe, deteriorating firefighter facilities, which will help improve emergency response times and protect the health and safety of our firefighters.
Key investments will include:
• Improving facilities and infrastructure to support rapid 911 emergency medical response, matching the standard of care available across the County.
• Bringing firefighter apparatus, equipment, and facilities up to current safety and industry standards.
• Rehabilitating unsafe firefighter housing, including removing mold and asbestos.
• Replacing deteriorating electrical systems, leaky pipes, roofs, and other aging infrastructure in fire stations.
• Bringing aging fire stations, some more than 80 years old, up to current building and safety codes.
• Improving the resiliency of fire stations and emergency response facilities during earthquakes, wildfires, and other disasters.
Measure Q requires strict accountability: independent financial audits and mandatory citizen oversight ensure every dollar is spent only on approved projects.

Richmond families deserve fast emergency response times and firefighters who are safe, equipped, and ready when they are needed most. Vote Yes on Measure Q to protect our neighbors, our first responders, and our community’s future.
Join Richmond firefighters, emergency medical responders, and neighbors across every district. Vote Yes on Measure Q.
United Business Organization, Juan Muñoz, President
St. Cornelius Catholic Church, Rev. Sergio Mora, Pastor
Myrtle L. Braxton, Senior Citizen
Karla M. Palma Melgar, Registered Nurse
Fernando Ramirez, Richmond Firefighter
arg_against: Vote No on Measure Q.
Richmond’s firefighters deserve safe, functional stations. Measure Q is the wrong way to pay for them.

Richmond property owners are already among the most heavily taxed in California. On top of the basic one percent rate, they pay roughly 0.42 percent more every year in voter-approved bond levies, over $420 per $100,000 of assessed value. West Contra Costa school bonds alone cost about $250 per $100,000, the highest school-bond rate in the county. Community college bonds, two BART bonds, and a regional park bond pile on further. Homeowners still pay a $52 hospital parcel tax for Doctors Medical Center, which closed in 2016 and was demolished. Enough is enough.

Measure Q involves borrowing $120 million and forces property owners to repay $249,749,206, more than double, with the tax collected all the way through 2060. You would pay for decades, at interest, to fix leaky roofs, old pipes, mold and electrical systems that ordinary budgeting should have maintained.

And Richmond does not need to borrow. The city just received the Chevron settlement, roughly $550 million over ten years. The entire fire-facility need it has identified is about $115 million. Two years of settlement money covers all of it, with no new tax and no interest.

The city knows this. When Councilmember Bana pressed for a backup plan, City Manager Shasa Curl confirmed that if voters say no, Richmond will simply use settlement funds to upgrade the stations. A no vote puts no firehouse at risk. Richmond’s own poll agrees: 81 percent said the city “should be more responsible and spend the money it already has.”
Fix the stations with the money already in hand. Do not pile another quarter-billion-dollar tax on property owners who already pay enough.
Vote No on Measure Q.
Contra Costa Taxpayers Association, Marc D. Joffe, President
Denise Gianni, Richmond Resident

title: Sales tax
question: To provide funding to maintain City services, including crime prevention, police protection, reducing illegal dumping, the City’s daily senior meal program, youth scholarship programs, assisting the homeless, street maintenance, and other general services, shall San Pablo enact a temporary ½-cent sales tax for 5 years, generating approximately $2,000,000 annually, then reduced to ¼-cent for 5 years, generating approximately $1,000,000 annually, then terminate; with all funds staying in San Pablo, citizen oversight, and mandated annual audits?
analysis: The San Pablo City Council placed Measure R on the ballot to ask voters to approve an increase to the City’s transactions and use tax, more commonly known as a local sales tax. Measure R would temporarily increase the local sales tax by 0.50% for five years, lower this increase by 0.25% for the next five years, and then expire after that ten-year period.

The sales tax generally applies to retail sales of tangible personal property within the City. Purchases that are exempt from the state sales tax are also exempt from the additional tax proposed here. For example, most groceries and prescription drugs are exempt from Measure R.

Currently, the total sales tax in San Pablo is 9.50% of an item’s purchase price. The City’s share of this is only 1.75%, with the remainder going to the state and to Contra Costa County. Part of the City’s share is the temporary sales tax most recently approved by the voters as Measure S in 2020. The tax imposed under Measure S is set to decrease next year and then expire five years after that. With Measure R’s own scheduled decrease and expiration, this means that, if voters approve Measure R, the total sales tax rate in San Pablo will change as follows:
• Immediately after Measure R’s approval, the total sales tax rate will increase to 10.00%.
• In October 2027, under Measure S’s scheduled decrease, the rate will lower to 9.75%.
• In October 2032, when Measure S expires and Measure R’s decrease goes into effect, the rate will lower to 9.25%.
• In 2037, when Measure R expires, the rate will lower again to 9.00%.

All revenues from Measure R would belong to the City and would be placed into the City’s general fund to be used for any lawful purpose. The City estimates the measure would bring in an additional $2,000,000 annually for the first five years, dropping to approximately $1,000,000 annually for the five years after that. Measure R must be approved by a simple majority (50% plus one) of the City’s voters. If approved, as noted above, it will expire after ten years.

Each year, an independent auditor must complete a public audit report of the revenues and expenditures from Measure R. The City Council is also required to appoint an oversight committee whose members are San Pablo residents or San Pablo business representatives. The oversight committee publicly reviews the audit report and makes recommendations on the use of the revenues. The audit report and the oversight committee’s recommendations would be a public record and reviewed at a public meeting.
A “yes” vote is to permit the City of San Pablo to increase its local sales tax for ten years.
A “no” vote is to prohibit the City of San Pablo from increasing its local sales tax.
Brian P. Hickey
City Attorney
Dated: August 19, 2026
arg_for: Vote Yes to keep San Pablo’s Essential services strong.
San Pablo is a great place to live. But the City faces real financial challenges. A Yes vote will help keep important services in place, including:
• Crime prevention and police protection
• Cleaning up and preventing illegal dumping
• Daily senior meal program
• Youth scholarship and recreation programs
• Street and road maintenance
• Rental and tenant protections
• Help for residents facing homelessness
Why is this measure needed:
Casino revenue is declining. It funds 59% of the City’s general fund and has fallen $3.3 million short since 2023.
Reserves are for catastrophic events and emergencies only; not for ongoing operating costs.
Everyone pays their fair share. Visitors who shop, buy gas, and eat here pay for it too.
Groceries and prescription medicines are not taxed.

The tax is temporary and shifts down, over time. A temporary half-cent sales tax for five years (yielding $2 million a year), then reduced to a quarter-cent for five years (yielding $1 million per year), then terminating. It cannot be extended without another vote of the people.
Every dollar stays in San Pablo. 100% of this revenue must remain here. By law, the State cannot take one penny of the yield.
Accountability is required, not promised. An independent Citizens’ Oversight Committee will review all spending; annual independent audits are mandatory and will be made public.

San Pablo’s sales tax rate remains among the lowest in West County. Even with Measure R, San Pablo remains below El Cerrito, Pinole, and Hercules. When previous adopted Measure S sales tax measure shifts down in October 2027, San Pablo ties Richmond for West County’s lowest sales tax rate.
A temporary, responsible solution. A modest amount to maintain what we already have: Local services. Local control. Local dollars.
Questions? Visit: www.sanpabloca.gov/2943
Vote Yes on Measure R
Genoveva Calloway, Registered Voter, Local Community Member
Dr. Raynato Castro, DDS., Registered Voter, Local Community Member/Medical Professional
Dorothy Gantt, Registered Voter, Local Community Member
Martin Gonzalez, Registered Voter, Local Community Member/Business Owner
Dr. William Van Dyke, DDS., Registered Voter, Local Community Member/Medical Professional
arg_against: Measure R’s ballot question lists budget line-items chosen to get more votes, appealing to those who like clean streets or freebies for seniors
and youth, prefer government to deal with the homeless, or dislike potholes or crime. Something for everyone.
They’re not supposed to take sides. Voters take sides.
Measure R does not guarantee what will be funded, as the question-wording implies.

The tax feeds the general fund spent on employee benefits and pensions, janitorial services, liability insurance, utility bills, consultants, legal fees, marketing materials, meeting expenses, holiday decorations, HVAC repairs, gasoline, window cleaning, toilet paper, and pay-raises.
They’re using the general fund to push voters to vote more funds. Is that okay?
Of course not.
California Elections Code section 13119(a) requires ballots to use this language:
“Shall the measure (stating the nature thereof) be adopted?”
Measure R used one word, “shall.” The rest are missing.
“The nature thereof” does not mean “why,” or “how,” or “for whom,” or anything other than “what is the nature” of the measure being adopted. It must be completely neutral.

Earlier this year when Contra Costa County wrote a ballot question promoting imposition of a sales tax increase, it was ruled “prejudicial and argumentative” in Superior Court. Offending language was removed, including “independent citizens oversight” (a committee not created by the measure).
The Measure R ballot question similarly mentions “citizen oversight” and mandated audits but these are already in place. It’s just a sales pitch.
As a plaintiff in the county case, I know the window of time to challenge these ballot-question violations is extremely short. [If you’re reading this, it’s too late.]
I don’t like public funds spent defending violations.
The best way to save court costs and stop the cheating is vote “No” every time you see a ballot question stuffed full of sales pitches.
Libertarian Party of Contra Costa County, Sandra Kallander, Chair

title: Rent stabilization ordinance
question: Shall the proposed ordinance, prohibiting residential real property rental rate increases for some rental units that exceed sixty percent of the Consumer Price Index increase or three percent, whichever is lower, establishing a process for consideration of additional rent increases, requiring City administration estimated to cost approximately $1,080,000 to $2,360,000 annually, funded by annual rental property owner fees, limiting the grounds for evicting tenants of some rental units, and enacting additional housing regulations, be adopted?
analysis: Measure S qualified for the November 2026 ballot by citizen petition. This measure would repeal the City of San Pablo’s existing tenant relocation assistance ordinance (San Pablo Municipal Code Chapter 8.05) and replace it with a new, much broader ordinance called the “San Pablo Rent Stabilization and Tenant Protections Ordinance”. The new ordinance would also effectively replace the City’s current just cause for eviction protections ordinance (San Pablo Municipal Code Chapter 9.70) and housing stability and anti-harassment protections ordinance (San Pablo Municipal Code Chapter 9.80).

The City’s current tenant relocation assistance ordinance applies relatively narrowly, only when the City orders a rental unit vacated because of serious code violations. In that situation, the owner must pay the displaced tenant relocation benefits equal to two months’ fair market rent. The City’s current just cause for eviction protections ordinance is consistent with state law and provides additional relocation benefits of two months’ rent for certain no-fault evictions.
The City’s current ordinances do not otherwise add to state law regarding limits to rent increases.

If approved, Measure S would roll back rents to the amount charged as of July 1, 2025, for existing tenancies, and then limit how much a landlord may raise rent each year – generally to 60 percent of the increase in the regional Consumer Price Index, with a maximum of 3 percent. The measure would confirm existing law to require landlords to have a specific, legally recognized reason before ending a tenancy, such as nonpayment of rent, the owner’s plan to move into the property, or a substantial renovation, and it would prescribe notice and procedural requirements for each. Relocation payments would apply more broadly than under current law, generally in an amount equal to four months’ fair market rent or $12,000, whichever is greater, with an additional payment for elderly, disabled, or terminally ill tenants.

The measure would also expand existing prohibitions on specified forms of landlord harassment, protect tenants’ ability to organize, and regulate agreements in which a landlord pays a tenant to move out. It would create fees, a hearing process, and civil remedies, including damages and attorney fees, to administer and enforce these provisions.

The City ordered a report on the measure’s fiscal impact pursuant to Elections Code Section 9212. That report estimates the administrative resources required to implement the new ordinance are expected to range from approximately 3.2 to 7.9 full-time-equivalent employees and $1.08 million to $2.36 million annually, funded by annual rental property owner fees.
A “yes” vote approves the revisions to the City of San Pablo’s tenant relocation assistance ordinance, and effectively replaces other related ordinances, as summarized above.
A “no” vote leaves the City of San Pablo’s current tenant relocation assistance ordinance, and other related ordinances, in place.
Brian P. Hickey
City Attorney
Dated: August 19, 2026
arg_for: A stable San Pablo is a safer San Pablo.
Our community is strongest when families can remain in their homes, children stay in the same schools, seniors can age in place, and neighbors continue looking out for one another.

Measure S will reduce homelessness and displacement of families in San Pablo by limiting rent increases to an amount that is fair to both tenants and landlords and by preventing evictions without a reason.
This will make our community safer.

Measure S is based on laws that have helped communities across California preserve stable neighborhoods by protecting working families, seniors, and longtime residents from being forced out by unreasonable rent increases.

This measure protects the people who make San Pablo home. It helps provide stability for renters while preserving the schools, small businesses, and community organizations that depend on long-term residents. That benefits everyone.

Everyone agrees we need to strengthen tenant protections. The steps taken by the City Council will not protect renters and mobile home park residents. Measure S establishes reasonable limits on annual rent increases for covered units and creates clear, fair rules that help families plan for the future instead of living with constant uncertainty.

The measure protects responsible landlords by allowing fair annual rent increases and providing a process to seek additional adjustments when justified. It balances the interests of tenants and property owners while strengthening the long-term stability of our community.
The city will charge landlords a rental housing fee to fund the administration of this measure. The cost of instability and losing the people who make San Pablo home is far greater.
Communities are defined by the people who live in them. This measure protects the character, stability, and future of our city.
Vote Yes on Measure S for a stable, safe San Pablo.
Schylon Stewart, San Pablo Resident
Ashley Quezada, San Pablo Resident
Mashel Lindstrom, San Pablo Resident
Rising Juntos, Rhea Elina Laughlin, Executive Director
Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment Action, David Sharples, Director
arg_against: Vote No on Measure S Initiative: San Pablo residents deserve housing policies that protect renters, support responsible housing providers, and strengthen our community. Measure S does not achieve that balance.

San Pablo Needs Local Solutions: San Pablo needs locally developed solutions that serve our local community, not policies promoted by outside special interest groups. Our residents deserve policies tailored to San Pablo, not a one-size-fits-all approach.

New Bureaucracy and Costs: Measure S creates a new, costly regulatory program. The City’s independent report estimates that implementing Measure S could require up to almost 8 full-time equivalent employees and cost up to $2.36 million annually. These funds could otherwise support public safety, street repairs, prevention of homelessness, and other essential City services.

Measure S Will Not Build New Homes: This measure does not create new housing; it does not increase San Pablo’s housing supply or directly contribute toward achieving the City’s state-mandated RHNA housingproduction goals. Additional regulations may discourage housing investment and could reduce the number of rental homes available.

Property Maintenance and Housing Quality: Research cited in the City’s analysis suggests that Measure S may reduce incentives for property improvements, potentially affecting housing quality and neighborhood conditions. Deteriorating conditions can contribute to blight and crime.

Measure S Burdens Housing Providers: This Measure adds costly new compliance requirements, fees, and relocation payments that can exceed $12,000, without proper exemptions for single-family homes or ADUs. These complex requirements will place a significant financial burden on small “mom-and-pop” housing providers.
Renters Deserve Real Solutions: San Pablo should focus on creating more affordable housing and developing its Rent Review program – a more meaningful, less costly alternative to rent control.
For more information:
https://www.sanpabloca.gov/2920/Housing-Stability-Hub
Vote No on Measure S
Elizabeth Pabon-Alvarado, Mayor, City of San Pablo
Rita Xavier, Vice-Mayor, City of San Pablo
Dorothy Gantt, Registered Voter and San Pablo Renter
David Alvarado, Elected Official and San Pablo Homeowner

title: Appointed city treasurer
question: Shall the office of the City Treasurer be appointive?
analysis: Measure T presents to the voters of Walnut Creek the question of whether the office of City Treasurer should be made an appointed position, with the City Manager having the authority to appoint the City Treasurer. Currently, the office of City Treasurer is an elected office. State law authorizes a city election on the issue of whether to make the office of city treasurer an appointed position. Measure T was placed on the ballot by the City Council through Resolution No. 26-31.

The office of City Treasurer is one of the offices that make up the government of general law cities in California. City treasurers are responsible for performing the duties set forth in Government Code Section 41001 et seq., including but not limited to receiving and safely keeping city funds, complying with laws governing the deposit and securing of public and city trust funds, implementing a system of accounting and auditing of bond funds held by the city, paying out of City money based on properly executed warrants, submitting monthly financial reports showing receipts, disbursements and fund balances, and performing the duties related to the collection of City taxes and license fees as prescribed by ordinance. In 2026, the Walnut Creek City Treasurer is responsible for management of approximately 145 million dollars in average daily funds.

City treasurers may be either elected or appointed. By state law, elected city treasurers must reside and be a registered voter in the city in which they hold office. There are no additional minimum qualifications required under state law for the position of an elected city treasurer. The city may approve job specifications and minimum educational and professional qualifications for an appointed city treasurer.

If a simple majority of voters vote “YES” on this measure, the office of City Treasurer in the City of Walnut Creek will become appointive and will no longer be elected by voters. The City Manager, as authorized by the Walnut Creek Municipal Code, would appoint the City Treasurer when the term of the current incumbent expires in December 2026 or if the voters elect a City Treasurer on November 3, 2026, in December 2030, or earlier if a vacancy in the office occurs. If this measure is approved, this measure would save future costs associated with candidate elections related the position of City Treasurer.
If a simple majority of voters vote “NO” on this measure, the office of City Treasurer in the City of Walnut Creek will continue to be elected by voters.
arg_for: Vote Yes on Measure T to improve the vital role of the Walnut Creek City Treasurer. The Walnut Creek City Council and currently elected City Treasurer, among others, urge your support.

Currently , the only requirement to be elected Walnut Creek City Treasurer, is to be “a registered voter” in our city. Measure T improves accountability and protects the City’s future by changing this position from an elected to an appointed position, ensuring that future city treasurers are qualified to serve, subject to proper criteria, screening and background checks.

Our city is in strong financial condition. And, it’s also true that Walnut Creek’s City Treasurer responsibilities have expanded significantly and become more complex, including today overseeing approximately $145 million in municipal investments. The City Treasurer should be, at a minimum, a finance professional with a college degree, preferably a CPA, experienced in standard government accounting procedures, automated accounting systems, records management, and state and federal finance compliance laws.

Per the California Municipal Treasurers Association, fewer than 10% of California’s 483 cities still locally elect their city treasurers. Voting Yes on T brings Walnut Creek in line with modern practices and over 90% of California cities that employ appointed city treasurers.
Passage of Measure T will:
• Authorize a smooth transition from an elected to an appointed City Treasurer by 2030.
• Ensure that future Walnut Creek City Treasurers are appointed by the City Manager based on established professional qualifications.
• Provide procedures so future Walnut Creek City Treasurers are qualified for and capably perform required duties of the position.

• Require close collaboration between the City Treasurer, Finance Department, City Manager, elected City Council and City Council Finance Committee, to ensure financial transparency and accountability.

The City has a long history of sound financial management, and a professionally appointed City Treasurer will help protect that. Please join the Walnut Creek City Council, current elected (30-year) City Treasurer Ron Cassano, advocates of quality local government, and residents across Walnut Creek Voting Yes on T to help keep our city strong.
Kevin Wilk, Mayor
Matt Francois, Mayor Pro Tem
Ron Cassano, City Treasurer
Susan Hildreth, Rossmoor Resident and Member, Measure O Citizens’ Oversight Committee
Audrey Gee, Board Chair, Chamber of Commerce (2023-2024), Attorney, and Walnut Creek Resident
arg_against: Measure T asks Walnut Creek voters to give up their right to elect the City Treasurer and hand that choice to the City Council. Vote no.

The Council argues that an appointed office would be less political, but appointment would place the choice in the hands of the body the Treasurer is meant to oversee. The Treasurer is the only financial officer who answers to residents rather than to the officials who authorize the spending. State law charges the Treasurer with assuring the proper handling of municipal funds, managing the city’s multimillion-dollar investment portfolio under a policy the Council adopts each year, and sitting on the committee that reviews the budget and the audit. Making the office appointive would let the
Council hires the person assigned to review the Council’s own accounts, and a Council that prefers a Treasurer who approves what it brings forward has every reason to hire one.

Walnut Creek voters have weighed this question before and rejected it, in 1956 and again in 1996. The Council notes that most other cities in the county appoint their treasurers, though common practice elsewhere is not evidence that the change would serve Walnut Creek taxpayers.

The change would also produce no meaningful savings. The seat sits on a ballot residents are already casting, and the Treasurer’s modest part-time stipend is unchanged whether the office is filled by election or by appointment. It would, however, weaken accountability. An elected Treasurer can question spending, borrowing, or investment risk and answers only to voters. An appointed Treasurer serves at the Council’s pleasure and can be replaced for raising concerns the Council would rather not hear. Keep the choice of Treasurer with the voters.
Vote no on Measure T.
Contra Costa Taxpayers Assn, Denise P Kalm, Vice President
Robert Marshall, Retired Businessman
German Eduardo Messidoro, Retired Court Interpreter, USDOJ

title: Senior mixed-use rezoning (N. California Blvd at Ygnacio Valley Rd)
question: Shall the measure amending the City of Walnut Creek General Plan , the North Downtown Specific Plan , and the Municipal Code to redesignate a 2.4 acre site at the northeast corner of North California Boulevard and Ygnacio Valley Road from office uses to mixed use residential uses, and to create a new Mixed Use Residential Senior & Commercial zoning district to limit allowable uses on the site to multifamily senior housing (primarily 55 years of age or older) and commercial uses compatible with senior housing, be adopted?
analysis: Measure U was placed on the ballot through a voter-sponsored petition signed by the requisite number of Walnut Creek voters. It proposes to amend the city’s General Plan, North Downtown Specific Plan (NDSP), and the zoning ordinance/zoning map to establish a new “Mixed Use – Residential Senior & Commercial” (MU-RSC) zoning district and to specifically rezone a 2.4-acre parcel at the northeast corner of North California Boulevard and Ygnacio Valley Road across from the Walnut Creek BART station to MU-RSC. The MU-RSC district would change the site’s current use from office to mixed-use residential, consisting primarily of senior housing serving primarily persons 55 years or older, residential care and congregate living facilities, supportive and accessory housing required by state law, and compatible commercial retail uses. Future projects in MU-RSC district may, but are not required to, develop any or all of these uses, with required senior housing.

The Measure does not propose a specific project in the MU-RSC, but sets a base density at 1 unit per 425 square feet of net lot area and increases the maximum floor area ratio for commercial uses to 0.6 from the current 0.3. The city’s inclusionary ordinance would require future senior residential projects to develop affordable units or pay an in-lieu fee. These inclusionary units can be used to qualify the project for additional density and incentives/concessions. Future senior housing will likely qualify for a density bonus pursuant to Government Code section 65915, which grants a default 20 percent bonus. If density-bonus eligible, the project can also request waivers of applicable city development and design standards, including reducing setbacks and exceeding Measure A height limit applicable to the 2.4-acre property. A future project may be subject to California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) review or may qualify for a CEQA exemption.

Absent voter approval or city approval of the landowner’s application, the city cannot substantively amend the MU-RSC or reduce its development capacities as they apply to 2.4-acre site. While the MU-RSC only includes the 2.4-acre site currently, other Walnut Creek properties could be rezoned to this zoning designation to utilize its development allowances, if approved by the city council.

A “Yes” vote is a vote to approve Measure U and its proposed amendments. A “No” vote is a vote against Measure U and the proposed amendments. Measure U will be approved if it receives a simple majority of “Yes” votes. If approved, Measure U would take effect on the earliest date legally possible. If the city has already made the maximum four general plan amendments allowed in a calendar year under state law, Measure U’s General Plan amendments would take effect on January 1 of the next year and its other amendments will take effect subject to this effective date as applicable.
arg_for: Walnut Creek is an amazing place to call home – and Measure U will help us keep it that way.

Seniors make up nearly half of Walnut Creek’s population, but with the lack of emphasis for new housing designated for seniors, many seniors and older adults are being pushed out further and further into the East Bay, away from their families, healthcare providers and communities, at an age where they need to find a place that supports their changing needs.

An independent review recently found that 44% of the households within 2 miles of North Downtown are occupied by seniors but only 5% of the total future homes in the area are specifically designated for seniors.

Passage of Measure U will be a crucial step forward by updating zoning in North Downtown Walnut Creek to permit over 200 units of high-quality senior housing and community-serving retail near BART – without raising taxes.

The project’s prime location next door to the Walnut Creek BART station offers easy access to regional destinations, local services, and the Downtown Trolley system. This promotes walkability, wellness, and independence, ensuring our seniors can stay connected without relying solely on a car.
Measure U facilitates a vibrant, mixed-use center which could include a multi-use market similar to the Rockridge Public Market/San Francsico Ferry Building or a full-service specialty market.

This initiative aligns with Walnut Creek’s General Plan, including the City’s recently adopted Housing Element and North Downtown Specific Plan. It advances Walnut Creek’s goals for sustainable growth, reduced traffic, and enhanced quality of life, and to begin to balance the supply of housing in Walnut Creek designated for seniors.

Measure U is a responsible, forward-thinking investment in Walnut Creek’s future. It provides the housing our seniors need while creating a thriving mixed-use area for everyone – without raising taxes.
Please join us, Yes on Measure U – https://www.wcseniorhousing.org/
Marlene R. Farrell, Friends of Walnut Creek Senior Housing
Stephen L. Kostka, Advocate for Senior Housing
Hailey Murphy, Walnut Creek Resident
arg_against: No Argument Against was filed.

title: Parcel tax increase
question: Shall the measure supporting high-quality education in local high schools by:
analysis: The governing board of the Acalanes Union High School District has adopted a resolution proposing a parcel tax (a qualified special tax).

If this measure passes, beginning on July 1, 2027, the current parcel tax would be increased by $168 annually on parcels of taxable real property within the District for eight years, expiring on June 30, 2035. Based on information from the County Auditor-Controller’s Office, there are two existing parcel taxes totaling $301 per parcel annually. If this measure passes, the total amount of annual parcel taxes would be $469 per parcel.

The parcel tax would apply to each parcel of taxable real property in the District. A parcel of taxable real property is any unit of real property in the District that receives a separate tax bill for property taxes from the Contra Costa County Treasurer-Tax Collector’s Office.

The ballot measure includes certain exemptions. Upon proper application to the District, the District may exempt any parcel from the parcel tax that is owned and occupied as a principal residence by (1) a person 65 years of age or older; (2) a person receiving Supplemental Security Income for a disability; or (3) a person receiving Social Security Disability Insurance benefits, whose yearly income does not exceed 250 percent of the 2012 federal poverty guidelines issued by the United States Department of Health and Human Services. Additionally, property that is otherwise exempt from property taxes shall also be exempt from the parcel tax.

The ballot measure states that the proceeds of the parcel tax will be used to support “high-quality education in local high schools by attracting/retaining highly qualified teachers; continuing advanced academic programs in science, technology, engineering, math and arts that prepare students for success in college and careers; [and] maintaining manageable class sizes.” Proceeds from the parcel tax may be used only for the specific purposes set forth in the ballot measure and according to constitutional and statutory provisions.

State law requires the District’s chief fiscal officer to file an annual report with the District’s governing board that states the amount of funds received and expended in each year and the status of any projects required or authorized to be funded from the parcel tax proceeds. State law also requires the proceeds from the parcel tax to be deposited into a separate designated account. The measure also would require the District to have an appointed citizens’ oversight committee to oversee the use of parcel tax proceeds.
Of those voting on the measure, two-thirds must approve the measure for it to pass.
A ”yes” vote is in favor of authorizing the parcel tax for an eight-year period.
A “no” vote is against authorizing the parcel tax for an eight-year period.
arg_for: Vote Yes on Measure W to protect the outstanding quality of education local high school students receive from Acalanes Union High School District schools.

Today’s high school graduates must be prepared to compete in a highly technical and competitive global workforce. Our four public high schools —Acalanes High School, Campolindo High School, Las Lomas High School, and Miramonte High School—have answered the educational call, today ranking among the top 5% of all high schools nationwide.
Here’s the problem: years of inadequate state funding have taken their toll. This is not an expense problem; it’s a revenue problem.

AUHSD’s last new funding measure was 16 years ago. While educational costs continue rising, AUHSD has cut $4.2M in the last 2 years alone! Without Measure W, drastic cuts will continue. Our students will suffer in academic program losses, increasing class sizes, and layoffs of valued teachers, counselors, and support staff.
Measure W will:
● Protect advanced science, technology, engineering, and math programs that help students get into college
● Retain/attract highly-qualified teachers
● Maintain manageable class sizes
● Preserve high-quality music, visual, and performing arts programs
● Continue Career Technical Education for in-demand fields like auto mechanics, fabrication, skilled trades, biotech, medical and health sciences
● Keep classroom technology/instructional materials current
● Provide academic intervention for students in need
● Restore positions lost to budget cuts – especially teachers, counselors, and school librarians.
Senior Citizens are eligible for exemption.

Mandatory Taxpayer Protections: No funds for administrators’ salaries; Citizens’ Oversight and independent audits ensure proper spending; Measure W lasts 8 years only; all funds stay local, benefitting AUHSD only.
Maintaining high-quality schools is a wise investment. Great schools protect property values and quality of life.
Teachers, parents, seniors, civic leaders and residents across our community are voting Yes . They know, as we do, the need is great and our kids are worth it!
Join us! Vote Yes on W!
www.YesForOurHighSchools.com
Matt Francois, Parent of Las Lomas Grads, Attorney, Walnut Creek City Councilmember & Former Mayor
Connie Collier, Local Business Owner, Diablo Foods, 58-yr. Lafayette Resident, Past PTA Pres.
Fred Weil, Taxation/Corp. Attorney, School Trustee (’79-2000), Co-Founder, Moraga Ed Found., 54-yr. Homeowner
Amy Worth, Former Orinda Mayor, 24-yr City Councilmember, 44-yr. Orinda Homeowner, Parent of Miramonte Grads
Dennis Fay, Rossmoor Resident, Former Orinda Mayor/Civic Leader, Retired Transportation Executive
arg_against: Just last year, the Acalanes Union High School District (AUHSD) spent $834,000 of taxpayer money on Measure T, a special election for a $130 parcel tax.
We rejected it.

The board’s response? Return to the ballot with a bigger tax, $168 per parcel for eight years, adding to the existing $301 parcel tax : same district, eighteen months later, demanding nearly 30% more than in Measure T.
But AUHSD doesn’t have a revenue problem; AUHSD has a spending problem.

State data show the District’s cost per student essentially doubling from 2012-13 to 2024-25, from $10,305 to $20,508 — a 99% jump, while Bay Area CPI inflation was only 45%. That’s unsustainable, and much of the increase never reached the classroom.
Where did it go?
• Wellness Centers on each high-school campus;
• A costly Central Administration;
• Non-academic Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging programming.

• AUHSD teaches seniors an elective Deconstructing Race course, grounded in Critical Race Theory , that could put federal funding at risk. And AUHSD voluntarily requires Ethnic Studies for graduation, though it is neither funded nor required by the state.
Such choices are unrelated to math, science, or teacher pay.
AUHSD is financed mainly by local property taxes that keep climbing with home values.
And California’s new budget handed AUHSD a one-time grant of nearly $5 million.
The money is there. The priorities are wrong.
AUHSD already collects two permanent parcel taxes , atop the hefty TK-8 parcel taxes we also pay.
Adding a third AUHSD tax rewards the same runaway spending.

Rather than cut administrative overhead or consolidate high schools with AUHSD’s feeder districts (as other communities have done to reduce spending), AUHSD’s Board is doubling down on duplicate bureaucracy.
Homeowner budgets are stressed enough already.
Don’t reward AUHSD’s runaway spending. Vote No on Measure W.
See StopMeasureW.com.
Contra Costa Taxpayers Association, Marc D. Joffe, President
Sarah Lind, Activist Mom and Small Business Owner, Lafayette
Jeff Frese, Father and Candidate for U.S. Congress, Moraga
Frank Darling, Father and Grandfather, Orinda
Kathleen Young, Mother and Grandmother, Walnut Creek

title: Bond measure
question: In order to repair and improve aging classrooms, fix deteriorating roofs, plumbing, heating, ventilation and electrical systems, remove asbestos/ lead pipes, upgrade science labs, libraries, technology and other facilities to support college/ career readiness in math, science, health, engineering, arts and skilled trades; shall Liberty Union High School District’s measure be adopted authorizing $165,000,000 in bonds at legal rates, levying $20 per $100,000 assessed value (raising $11,300,000 annually) while bonds are outstanding and all funds benefiting local schools?
analysis: The California Constitution provides that school districts may issue bonds for the construction, reconstruction, rehabilitation or replacement of school facilities, including the furnishing and equipping of school facilities or the acquisition or lease of real property for school facilities, with the approval of 55% of the voters voting at an election for that purpose.

By resolution, the Liberty Union High School District has proposed that bonds of the District be issued in an amount up to $165,000,000. The measure provides that proceeds from the sale of the bonds will be used to “repair and improve aging classrooms, fix deteriorating roofs, plumbing, heating, ventilation, and electrical systems, remove asbestos/lead pipes, upgrade science labs, libraries, technology and other facilities to support college/career readiness in math, science, health, engineering, arts and skilled trades.” The specific projects are set forth in the bond project list within the measure. The measure provides that a citizens’ oversight committee will be established to ensure that bond proceeds are properly expended and that annual performance and financial audits will be conducted. The measure further provides that bond proceeds will only be used for the purposes specified in the measure and not for any other purpose.

Approval of this measure authorizes levy upon taxable property in the district to repay the bonded indebtedness, both principal and interest, in each year that the bonds are outstanding. The Liberty Union High School District has prepared a Tax Rate Statement, which represents the District’s best estimates of the property tax rates required to service the bonds. The estimated highest annual tax rate required to be levied to fund the bonds is expected to be $20 per $100,000 of assessed valuation.

Approval of the measure does not guarantee that the proposed project or projects in the District that are the subject of the bonds under the measure will be funded beyond the local revenues generated by the measure. The proposed project or projects may assume receipt of matching state funds, which could be subject to appropriation by the Legislature or approval of a statewide bond measure.
Of those voting on the measure, 55% must approve the measure for it to pass.
A ”yes” vote is in favor of authorizing the bonded indebtedness.
A “no” vote is against authorizing the bonded indebtedness.
arg_for: Our high schools are among the best in the region. Liberty, Freedom, and Heritage High Schools provide outstanding instruction that prepares students for college, careers, and lucrative jobs. All three schools have earned recognition as California Distinguished Schools and California Gold Ribbon Schools.

To maintain that standard, Measure X will fund critical repairs and upgrades needed for student success. Many facilities are more than 60 years old. Aging infrastructure has caused gas leaks, water leaks, sewage backups, and more than 150 roof leaks in the past two years alone. These problems must be addressed.
Top Priority projects have been identified at each school, including:
Removing hazardous materials such as asbestos and lead pipes from older schools
Upgrading campuses to meet current health, safety, and accessibility standards
Repairing or replacing deteriorating roofs, plumbing, gas lines, sewer lines, heating, ventilation, electrical systems, and aging portables
Providing modern classrooms, technology, and facilities that support instruction in math, science, engineering, and technology
Expanding career technical education with updated labs and equipment for programs such as health sciences, agriculture, skilled trades, law enforcement, and fire safety
Improving student safety through upgraded fencing, cameras, emergency communication systems, smoke detectors, fire alarms, and sprinklers
Every penny from Measure X will stay in our community and cannot be used for salaries. Independent citizens’ oversight and annual audits are required to ensure funds are spent as promised.

Whether or not you have children in our schools, strong local schools protect our quality of life and support property values. If approved, Measure X will bring up to $35 million in state matching funds to our district that would otherwise go elsewhere, maximizing the value of local taxpayer dollars.
Measure X will protect our schools, improve student safety, modernize aging facilities, and secure additional state funding for our community.
Please vote Yes on Measure X.

arg_against: Vote No on Measure X because now is not the time to worsen East Contra Costa affordability.

Measure X increases costs for residents by $350 million of total debt service through 2058. Liberty Union High School District (LUHSD) is still paying off existing construction/maintenance bonds of Measure U (2016, $122 million, payoff 2047) and Measure A (2001, $65.4 million, payoff 2030).
A $700,000 assessed value home now pays $178.50 annually for these two bonds. Measure X’s payoff, adding another $140.00 assessment, makes the total $318.50.
LUHSD enrollment is flat, just 0.34% higher than 2016’s. So new bond funds would be used for maintenance and nice-to-have enhancements, not increased instructional capacity.
Vote No on Measure X because the expenditures are unaccountable.

In 2016 voters approved Measure U , borrowing $122 million (plus interest) to include maintenance issues similar to those cited now. Measure U was supposed to fix deteriorating roofs, plumbing, HVAC, electrical wiring, etc. Yet Measure X repeats those fixes now.

Measure X’s project list is a catch-all, not a plan. “Repair and improve aging classrooms,” “upgrade… other facilities,” and college/career readiness “in math, science, health, engineering, arts and skilled trades” covers virtually any expenditure. Voters are being asked to approve $165 million (plus $185 million interest) without a prioritized project list.
Measure X’s cited costs are “based upon projections and estimates only… and are not binding upon the District.” If home values drop, bond-payback tax rates could increase.
Vote No because Measure X’s project list isn’t sufficiently specific.

California’s Constitution requires “A list of the specific school facilities projects to be funded….” Measure X ‘s Bond Project List states “The items presented on the following list provide are (sic) the types of projects authorized…. Examples included… are not intended to limit the broader types of projects described and authorized by this measure.” Sorry, that’s not specific.

Kathleen E. Griffin, 29-year Brentwood Resident
Tracy M Kasamoto, Retired, Courtroom Deputy Clerk
